KIARASH TAHERI / RESIDENTIAL / DESIGN 5

Residence
Hell.

From a question drawn on paper to a design system that can grow, be interrupted, and make architecture.

Original residential sketch / May 2026
00 / THE PROJECT

A residential project became a way to test who makes a spatial decision.

The Shahrak Gharb brief began with a site and a housing question. Sketches and Grasshopper experiments asked how households, cores, gardens, light and circulation might affect one another. Residential grew into a workspace for setting rules, watching a run, and changing it while it is still forming.

The records below come from different moments and runs. Captions distinguish the saved Shahrak case, synthetic demonstrations and proposed construction work.

01 / THE CURRENT INSTRUMENT

First, see what the system makes.

A saved 100-home Shahrak case becomes a spatial model and a working interface. The model image is a render of the recorded case; the screen below is a later live capture of the full application.

THE WORKSPACE / ACTUAL APPLICATION

Site inputs, model canvas, analysis and the growth programme are visible together. Open the full capture to inspect the controls.

02 / ORIGIN

Questions before a generator.

Notebook work, a complete parametric definition, optimization trials and a debugging state show the questions and difficulties that preceded the current workspace.

03 / SYSTEM

A programme of decisions, with places to intervene.

The saved C01 run did not appear in one step. It placed households, checked stranded agents, built circulation, and added gardens and sitework. These four images are individual saved checkpoints.

THE SAVED PROGRAMME / 11 STAGES
  1. Neighbourhood blocks
  2. Reserve corridors
  3. Place neighbourhoods
  4. Evaluate
  5. Circulation
  6. Stranded-agent check
  7. Cleanup
  8. Balconies
  9. Macro plan
  10. Gardens
  11. Sitework
ONE RECORDED CHOICE

Three valid places for one home.

A later engine replay used the saved C01 checkpoint-6 geometry to test household 036. It found 36 valid candidates. The three shown are the leading pair and a distinct location in that replay; they are not a reconstruction of the historical decision.

Scores describe this later replay on unchanged C01 geometry. They are not a judgment of lived quality or proof that the original historical ranking was reproduced.

A NEW RUN IN THE LIVE WORKSPACE

Set a brief. Watch it grow. Check the result.

This 14-second sequence uses sampled frames from a live session: set 18 homes and a family-focused scheme on a 13 × 19 × 6 grid, choose the courtyard policy, then grow the model. The policy reserves a central void before placing homes, routing access and adding gardens. Winter and summer sun lenses are inspected afterward. This is a separate software demonstration, not another view of the saved Shahrak case.

04 / GROWTH

Watch a run take shape.

Move through 113 retained C01 placement states. Every frame is saved geometry; the control does not invent steps between them.

C01 / PLACEMENT RECORD001 / 113
BEYOND ONE RUN

Different inputs, different configurations.

These six saved synthetic requests are compact range samples, not successive C01 frames or outcomes of the Shahrak brief.

05 / AUTHORSHIP

Pause. Change the field. Continue.

A separate six-home demonstration records a human edit to an active run. After two homes are placed, five cells are reserved and one home is locked. The branch continues around those decisions.

The reserved footprint is an input to this recorded synthetic run, not a built slab.

06 / ANALYSIS

Read the same Shahrak model through different fields.

These eight retained application views keep the actual housing arrangement in place while the selected lens changes. They show the recorded design in context, including terrain, roads, planting and surrounding fabric. The color scales are software analysis views, not measured post-occupancy performance.

UNDER THE MODEL VIEW

Ten recorded values across occupied homes.

The saved C01 field cache contains ten normalized channels. Each axonometric drawing colors the occupied home cells by one recorded field value at its actual grid level, so the same Shahrak mass can be compared across ten readings. It is a source-derived analytical projection, not a new run or a building performance certificate.

The eight original views and ten-channel cache are different retained records of the Shahrak work. Colors and normalized values explain relative model quantities; they do not establish observed environmental conditions.

07 / ARCHITECTURE

The saved Shahrak case has more than a plan.

The retained material includes a 100-home Shahrak design, its sectional and site drawings, an earlier C01 export, and later modeled dwelling studies. Captions identify each record and its origin. None depicts a built place.

RESIDENCE HELL / KIARASH TAHERI
The pavilion we built for Harakat, May 2025.
02 / built / may 2025

Wood–Thread
Pavilion.

I designed the pavilion in Rhino and Grasshopper for the Architecture Scientific Association’s Harakat Festival booth. In May 2025, we cut it, put up the frame and threaded it together.

builtparametricfabrication
Design / buildI designed and modelled the pavilion; putting it together was a group effort.
BUILT IN THE PARK

A field of thread in the park.

The frame rises and falls across the park. Orange and pale threads cross, tighten and open again. Looking at it afterwards, I saw how much movement was already in it: harekat, the name of the festival.

MATERIAL / WEAVING

Starting with the loom.

Carpet weaving was one of the things I had in mind. At the loom, many separate threads are held together by a frame. In the pavilion, they stretch between timber members and open out into space.

I photographed the loom on a trip to Bijar. The yarn photograph is a colour reference, not a record of the material we bought.
FORM / FRAME

What holds the threads.

Under the light thread field are plywood bases and angled timber members. The model lets you see how they meet. B02 and B03 are the two base types shown here; their flat cuts appear with the making drawings below.

The assembled views leave out some of the flat cuts. The exploded views separate the parts so they can be read; they do not show the order in which we built them.

GRASSHOPPER / THE DEFINITION

The pattern was not drawn line by line.

In Grasshopper, support curves lead to ordered points and then to selected connections between them. I have kept the saved graph in one view, so you can follow the whole definition rather than a few isolated fragments.

01 / Set the supports

Curves and guides place the members and set the edges of the field.

02 / Order the points

Division and sorting give the points along those edges an order.

03 / Connect them

Line, weave and cull operations determine which paths remain in the saved preview.

In the Rhino file, each of the 101 thread objects has two separate shells. The 202 paths traced from them are model geometry, not the number of threads we wound or a threading schedule.

SAVED CONFIGURATIONS

Variations, together.

Fourteen configurations survive in the model. Together, they show how the slope, crossing and density could change. The photographs on this page show the piece we actually built.

Assembly

Then we had to make it stand.

The sheets and profiles show the cuts behind the frame. In the photographs, the bases and angled members are already standing, ready for the threads to be drawn between them.

01 / PARTS ON THE SHEET

The base renders leave out some slots. In the flat drawings, the cuts are much easier to see. I have put the drawings together at the same scale of attention; their geometry is unchanged.

Stock sheets

N01–N08 / saved cutting layouts

Base part contours

F01–F05 / the same cut curves, arranged so the parts can be compared

Timber members

M01–M05 / member lengths and two rows of holes

These circles are Ø6 mm in the saved drawing. The file does not tell us the final drilling depth or method.

02 / IN THE PARK

Then the flat parts became a standing frame. These photographs show the bases and timber before the thread field went in.

RESULT / MAKING

The pavilion in motion.

My hand moves through the finished threads. The camera travels across the whole piece, returns to the night we threaded it, then comes back into the daylight.

RHINO / INTERACTIVE VIEW

Turn the model around.

The photographs flatten some of the relationships between the bases, uprights and thread field. Here you can move around the design and see them from another side.

This browser version simplifies the Rhino geometry. It shows the saved design, not a survey of the finished structure.

Built field

Where the threads meet.

After the full view, I wanted to get close to the actual strands: where they rise from a base, where the colours cross, and finally the ladybug among them.

KIARASH TAHERI / NEUROARCHITECTURE

Space.
Body.
Signal.

Research method, a programmable study instrument, and a physical EEG–VR pilot.

Research assistant to Dr. Boshra Abbasi
01 Question02 Instrument03 Co-wear04 Sequence05 Readout06 Next study
01 / RESEARCH QUESTION

What does a spatial change do to experience?

Define the change. Then connect the delivered scene to a participant's report, behavior, and EEG window.

01Specify one architectural contrastHold the route and other scene conditions steady.
02Know what was deliveredPreserve the version, order, timing, and apparatus state.
03Compare several responsesRead report, behavior, and physiology together.

Method direction, not a participant result. Open the complete research drawing ↗

02 / PROGRAMMABLE INSTRUMENT

From authored study to inspectable record.

NeuroArch connects study authoring, a frozen run plan, execution, retained source data, and review.

ACTUAL SOFTWARE / QA RECORDS

Three views from the running software, selected for what they visibly show.

Software screens document interface behavior. They do not establish headset display timing or physical EEG synchronization.

03 / PHYSICAL PILOT · 31 AUG 2026

The apparatus enters the measurement.

EEG electrodes, cables, and VR straps occupy the same head. A single-participant technical pilot examined co-wear and signal behavior.

1participant
64EEG channels
250 Hzsample rate
32:17native record
Contact is local.The analysis distinguishes superior and lateral strap-adjacent corridors. These schematic regions are not pressure measurements.Inspect original zone vector ↗
04 / RECONSTRUCTED SEQUENCE

What changed, and when?

Eight named intervals sit within one fixed-order recording. The source distinguishes nominal intervals from trimmed descriptive windows.

964 snamed condition intervals
884 sselected spectral windows

Source labels do not establish physical display onset. The final movement block's eye state was not specified.

05 / PILOT READOUT

Read the signal through the apparatus.

Descriptive checks from one person and one pass identify what the next protocol must control.

01 / DONNING

A physical transition appears in the signal.

Several summaries change around apparent headset donning, then settle. This supports an apparatus check, not an architectural effect.

02 / BASELINE

A physiological anchor.

Eyes closed versus open shows posterior alpha in this pilot. The topography checks recognizable signal structure.

03 / CONDITIONS

One sequence cannot isolate a room.

Posterior alpha varies across nominal intervals, but order, apparatus, movement, and scene remain entangled.

INTERPRETATION LIMITOne participant · one fixed order · no measured visual onset. This pilot guides protocol design; it does not establish a causal architectural response.
06 / NEXT STUDY · PROPOSED

Make the spatial claim answerable.

Define one room contrast, balance its exposure order, repeat baseline anchors, and measure the physical timing path.

01One designed contrastKeep spatial base and route constant.
02Balanced orderEvery condition appears at every position.
03Measured onsetAlign software event, display sensor, and EEG clock.

Universal Joints / folded source-part assembly study
STRUCTURAL KIT / DESIGN + PRINTING + ASSEMBLY

Universal Joints.

I designed and printed the six-way nodes, sphere-ended rods, thread clips and bracing bars, then built them into a frame. I kept adjusting the parts through repeated print trials. The rods can pivot at the nodes; the thread works in tension and the clip-ended bars in compression.

Designed + built3D printingStructural system
01 / BUILT SYSTEM

From a joint to a frame.

I assembled the kit in different configurations. The white rods and nodes make the frame; orange thread and gray clip-ended bars brace selected parts of it.

02 / ASSEMBLY STUDY

Make the connection.

Orbit the frame, place a node, seat a sphere-ended member, then add an orange thread tie or a gray two-grip bar at node edges. The four printed parts are taken from the saved Rhino model.

VIEW

BUILD WITH THE PRINTED PARTS

Choose a part, click a node to reveal its contacts, then build the connection. Drag to orbit; scroll or pinch to zoom.

This is an interactive assembly study using the saved part meshes. The angle control illustrates the joints’ movement; it is not a force simulation or a verified fit test.

03 / CONNECTION

Three kinds of contact.

Six bowl sockets turn the node outward in every direction. A sphere at each end of the main rod sits in a bowl and lets the rod change angle. Small clips grip the designated node edges: their closed eyes carry the orange thread loops. The long gray bars use open C grips at both ends.

04 / PRINTING + ADJUSTMENT

The connection took trials.

A printed joint needs to fit, release and hold in the hand, not just look right in a model. I printed it repeatedly, changed settings and made small adjustments before assembling the larger frame.

Two retained print setups

Two saved slicer projects, with creation metadata dated 26 December 2023 and 24 January 2024, retain different settings:

Layer height
0.20 / 0.10 mm
Bed temperature
60 / 70°C
Support interface
3 / 1 layers
Support spacing
2.5 / 5 mm

These files capture two settings among repeated print and fit trials; their metadata is not a complete making timeline.

05 / SPATIAL SYSTEM

Beyond the square bay.

The same joints can produce a folded field rather than a regular grid. Here the rows change direction in plan and section, while every member keeps the original saved span.

05 / ROBOTIC CONSTRUCTION LOGIC

One arm holds. The other joins.

One robot holds a timber in position; the other approaches its connection. The opposed rail cell followed a failed single-arm trial. These are proposed tools and motions, not a commissioned machine.

Saved concept geometry: a 5 mm stepped bracket and retained clamp shoe. The nominal post screws sit at Z = 260 mm, 40 mm apart; the base screws at Z = 150 mm, 70 mm apart. The upper screw position was rejected because the clamp blocks it. Fastening capacity is unverified.

A / Position + hold

Hold-and-join / proposed operation at a member connection

B / Joining access

A second moving arm is proposed to reach the connection while the first retains the timber pose.

Tool studies

Gripper contact and a nominal screw approach are modeled as concept hardware. Capacity and fastening remain unqualified.

The robot views retain their saved colors. The adjacent plan projects rail extents and one sampled tool path. The cell was not fabricated. Open original cell model view ↗
